evidence.excerpt: Clinical risk scores are expected to behave monotonically with respect to certain predictors: higher creatinine should not decrease predicted renal failure risk, for example. Unconstrained gradient boosted trees frequently violate such expectations, reducing clinician trust. This study applied monotonicity constraints available in the XGBoost and LightGBM libraries to three clinical risk modelling tasks: 30-day hospital readmission (n=7,940), acute kidney injury within 48 hours of ICU admission (n=3,210), and postoperative pulmonary complication (n=2,880). Constraint specifications were derived from a literature review and validated with three clinicians. Constrained models showed AUPRC reductions of 0.01 to 0.03 relative to unconstrained models, while achieving full monotonicity compliance on all constrained features. A clinician survey conducted after model demonstration rated constrained models as significantly more trustworthy on a five-point Likert scale (mean 4.1 vs 3.0, p < 0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). The trade-off between performance and interpretability was assessed using a proposed composite score.
